title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Deep layers. Transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, parietal peritoneum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inguinal canal. Oblique passage above the medial inguinal ligament from the deep ring (transversalis fascia) to the superficial ring (external oblique aponeurosis).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Flat muscles. External oblique (down and medially), internal oblique, transversus abdominis; their aponeuroses form the rectus sheath.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Rectus sheath. Envelops rectus abdominis; below the arcuate line all aponeuroses pass in front, leaving only transversalis fascia behind. Aponeuroses meet in the midline at the linea alba.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Superficial layers. Skin, fatty Camper's fascia and membranous Scarpa's fascia.

title: Rule of 3 of the anterolateral wall?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: Rule of 3 of the anterolateral wall?
body.back: Above muscles: skin, Camper's, Scarpa's. Muscles: EO, IO, TA. Below: transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, peritoneum.

title: Structures formed by the flat muscles?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: Structures formed by the flat muscles?
body.back: EO: inguinal ligament, superficial ring. IO: cremaster. IO + TA: conjoint tendon. Aponeuroses: rectus sheath, linea alba.
Aponeuroses envelop rectus; below the arcuate line all pass anteriorly, leaving transversalis fascia behind.
Umbilical vein → round ligament of liver; urachus → median umbilical ligament; umbilical arteries → medial umbilical ligaments.
Superficial: above umbilicus → axillary; below → superficial inguinal. Deep: internal thoracic, lumbar, external iliac.
Anterior: EO aponeurosis. Posterior: transversalis fascia (+ conjoint tendon). Roof: IO and TA arching fibres. Floor: inguinal (+ lacunar) ligament.
Male: spermatic cord. Female: round ligament. Both: ilio-inguinal nerve, genital branch of genitofemoral nerve.
Indirect: through deep ring, lateral to inferior epigastric vessels. Direct: through posterior wall, medial to them.
Psoas major/minor (medial), quadratus lumborum (lateral), iliacus (inferior), diaphragm (superior).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ampulla. Joins the pancreatic duct and opens at the major duodenal papilla; the sphincter of Oddi controls release.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Common bile duct. Common hepatic + cystic ducts; runs in the hepatoduodenal ligament, behind the duodenum, then through the pancreatic head.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Common hepatic duct. Formed at the biliary confluence at the hilum, within the hilar plate.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gallbladder. Pear-shaped sac under segments 4b-5 that stores and concentrates bile; the cystic duct has the spiral valve of Heister.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Left hepatic duct. Long extrahepatic course under the quadrate lobe, useful for surgical repairs.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Right hepatic duct. Short extrahepatic course; lies over the origin of the right portal vein.
Water, electrolytes, bile acids, cholesterol, phospholipids, bilirubin; 600-1000 mL/day; stored in gallbladder; enterohepatic circulation via ileum.
Right and left hepatic ducts join at the hilum over the right portal vein origin, within the hilar plate; left duct long, right short.

title: Course of the common bile duct?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: Course of the common bile duct?
body.back: Hepatoduodenal ligament → retroduodenal → intrapancreatic → hepatopancreatic ampulla → major papilla of D2.
Pear-shaped under segments 4b-5; fundus, body, neck; cystic duct with valve of Heister.
Liver, cystic duct, common hepatic duct; crossed by the cystic artery; critical view of safety before clipping.

title: Blood supply of the biliary tree?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: Blood supply of the biliary tree?
body.back: Hepatic arteries (intrahepatic, confluence), right hepatic + gastroduodenal + pancreaticoduodenal (CBD), cystic artery (gallbladder).
Sympathetic (storage, visceral pain), vagal (release), right phrenic (Glisson's capsule, somatic pain).
Cystic → hepatic → coeliac; pyloric → peripancreatic → mesenteric nodes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inferior mesenteric artery. Supplies the distal third of the transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, and upper rectum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: IMA branches. Left colic (descending colon), sigmoid arteries, superior rectal artery (upper rectum).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Marginal artery. Continuous arcade along the colon connecting SMA and IMA territories.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ileocolic artery. Caecum, appendix (appendicular artery in the mesoappendix), terminal ileum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Right colic artery. Ascending colon.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Middle colic artery. Transverse colon, in the transverse mesocolon.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Superior mesenteric artery. Supplies the caecum, appendix, ascending colon and proximal two thirds of the transverse colon.
Water absorption, vitamin K and B production, faeces compaction and storage, propulsion.
Taeniae coli, haustra, omental (epiploic) appendices.
Caecum: right iliac fossa (75%), intraperitoneal. Appendix: 6-10 cm, base at the convergence of taeniae, McBurney's point, variable tip, mesoappendix.

title: Parts of the colon in order?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: Parts of the colon in order?
body.back: Caecum, ascending, hepatic flexure, transverse, splenic flexure, descending, sigmoid.
Mobile: transverse (mesocolon), sigmoid (mesocolon). Fixed: ascending, descending (retroperitoneal).
SMA: ileocolic, right colic, middle colic. IMA: left colic, sigmoid, superior rectal. Marginal artery connects them.
Epicolic → paracolic → intermediate (ileocolic, mesocolic, sigmoid) → superior/inferior mesenteric nodes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Left hemiliver. Segments 2 and 3 (left lateral sector) and segment 4 (left medial sector).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Left hepatic vein and umbilical fissure. Separate the left lateral from the left medial sector.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Main portal fissure. Plane of the middle hepatic vein from the gallbladder fossa to the IVC, dividing right and left hemilivers.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Right hepatic vein. Runs in the right portal fissure between right sectors.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Right hemiliver. Segments 5 and 8 (right medial/anterior sector) and 6 and 7 (right lateral/posterior sector).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Segment 1. The caudate lobe, drained directly into the IVC, independent of both hemilivers.
Largest abdominal organ (~2% body weight); metabolic, detoxification, bile, glycogen; double inflow and outflow.
Mostly right hypochondrium; upper border 5th right rib → 6th left rib; inferior border from 10th right costal cartilage.
Diaphragmatic, visceral (gallbladder, porta hepatis, organ impressions), posterior (bare area, IVC groove).
Falciform, round (umbilical vein), coronary, triangular, lesser omentum, ligamentum venosum (ductus venosus).
Right, left, quadrate (between gallbladder and teres), caudate (between IVC and ligamentum venosum).
Carries the portal triad to the hilum; omental foramen behind; Pringle manoeuvre.
Oesophageal, paraumbilical, rectal, retroperitoneal; dilate in portal hypertension.
2 hemilivers (middle hepatic vein), 4 sectors, 8 segments; segment 1 = caudate; basis of liver resection.
Hepatic plexus (coeliac, SMA sympathetics; vagal parasympathetics); intercostals to Glisson's capsule; lymph to abdominal and mediastinal nodes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Greater splanchnic nerve. Preganglionic sympathetic fibres from T5-T9 synapsing in the coeliac ganglion (foregut).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lesser and least splanchnic nerves. T10-T11 to the superior mesenteric ganglion (midgut); T12 to the aorticorenal ganglion (kidney).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lumbar splanchnic nerves. L1-L2 to the inferior mesenteric ganglion and hypogastric plexuses (hindgut, pelvis).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pelvic splanchnic nerves. S2-S4 parasympathetic to the distal transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, bladder and reproductive organs.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Vagus nerve. Parasympathetic to the foregut and midgut up to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon.
Fluid balance, immune surveillance, fat absorption (chylomicrons via lacteals).
Parietal follow veins (inguinal, iliac, lumbar); visceral follow arteries to pre-aortic nodes.
Foregut → coeliac; midgut → superior mesenteric; hindgut → inferior mesenteric.
Lumbar trunks converge at L1-L2 (5-7 cm sac) → thoracic duct at T12 → left subclavian vein.
Longitudinal submucosal network; upper → deep cervical, middle → mediastinal, lower → left gastric/coeliac.

title: Somatic nerves of the abdominal wall?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: Somatic nerves of the abdominal wall?
body.back: Thoracoabdominal T7-T11, subcostal T12, iliohypogastric L1, ilio-inguinal L1, genitofemoral L1-L2.
Greater T5-T9 → coeliac; lesser T10-T11 → superior mesenteric; least T12 → aorticorenal; lumbar L1-L2 → inferior mesenteric.
Vagus: foregut and midgut to 2/3 transverse colon. Pelvic splanchnics S2-S4: hindgut, bladder, genitals.
Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus: motility. Submucosal (Meissner) plexus: secretion and blood flow.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Body. Crosses the aorta and L2 above the transpyloric plane; its peritoneal front forms the stomach bed; behind lie aorta, left adrenal, kidney and renal vessels.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Duct system. Main duct (Wirsung) from tail to head joins the bile duct at the ampulla (Vater); accessory duct (Santorini) opens at the minor papilla.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Head. Embraced by the C of the duodenum, right of the SMV; rests on the IVC and left renal vein; the bile duct grooves its posterosuperior surface.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Neck. Short; the portal vein forms behind it from the SMV and splenic vein.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Tail. Mobile, in the splenorenal ligament with the splenic vessels, reaching the splenic hilum near the left colic flexure.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Uncinate process. Hooks medially behind the superior mesenteric vessels.
12-20 cm, retroperitoneal, in front of L1-L2, between duodenum and spleen; exocrine acini and endocrine islets.
Head, uncinate process, neck, body, tail.
Head: duodenal C, CBD, IVC. Uncinate: behind SMA/SMV. Neck: over portal vein. Body: over aorta/L2, stomach bed. Tail: splenorenal ligament, splenic hilum.
Main (Wirsung) + CBD → ampulla of Vater → major papilla (sphincter of Oddi). Accessory (Santorini) → minor papilla.
Annular pancreas (ventral bud rotation failure); pancreas divisum (no duct communication).
Head: superior pancreaticoduodenal (GDA) + inferior pancreaticoduodenal (SMA) arcades. Body/tail: splenic branches.
Head → SMV and portal vein; body/tail → splenic vein; lymph with arteries to coeliac and SMA nodes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anterior division, visceral branches. Umbilical artery (superior vesical; its obliterated end is the medial umbilical ligament), inferior vesical in males or vaginal in females, uterine, middle rectal.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anterior division, other branches. Obturator (through the obturator canal to the medial thigh), internal pudendal (out through the greater, back through the lesser sciatic foramen to the perineum), inferior gluteal.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Internal iliac artery. Arises at the sacroiliac joint (L5/S1), about 4 cm long, and divides into anterior and posterior divisions.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Posterior division. Parietal only: iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal.
Inlet: promontory, iliopectineal line, symphysis. Outlet: coccyx, ischial tuberosities, pubic arch. False pelvis above brim; true pelvis below.
Aorta bifurcates at L4; common iliac divides at L5/S1 into external (→ femoral) and internal iliac.
Superior vesical (umbilical), inferior vesical/vaginal, uterine, middle rectal, obturator, internal pudendal, inferior gluteal.
Iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal (all parietal).
Uterine artery crosses over the ureter near the cervix: risk in hysterectomy.
Vesical, prostatic, uterine, vaginal, sacral, rectal (superior → portal; middle/inferior → systemic).
External iliac, internal iliac, obturator, presacral → common iliac → para-aortic.
T10-L2 → lumbar splanchnics → superior hypogastric → hypogastric nerves → inferior hypogastric; storage, ejaculation, bladder neck closure, IAS contraction.
S2-S4 pelvic splanchnics → inferior hypogastric; micturition, defecation, erection, secretion.
Above S2: spastic neurogenic bladder. S2-S4: flaccid bladder, overflow incontinence.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anal triangle. Posterior triangle containing the anal canal, the external anal sphincter and the fat-filled ischioanal fossae.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Perineal body. Fibromuscular node between the two triangles where many perineal muscles attach; its damage in childbirth weakens support.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pelvic diaphragm. Levator ani and coccygeus form the muscular floor separating the pelvic cavity from the perineum and supporting the pelvic organs.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Urogenital triangle. Anterior triangle between the ischiopubic rami; superficial perineal space and deep perineal space (external urethral sphincter, deep transverse perineal muscle).
Muscular-fascial floor separating the pelvic cavity from the perineum: levator ani + coccygeus.

title: Functions of the perineum and pelvic floor?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: Functions of the perineum and pelvic floor?
body.back: Support of pelvic organs, control of urination and defecation, sexual function.
Urogenital (anterior) and anal (posterior), divided by a line between the ischial tuberosities.
Superficial: ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus, superficial transverse perineal, erectile tissue. Deep: external urethral sphincter, deep transverse perineal.
Puborectalis (anorectal sling), pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus.
Central fibromuscular node where perineal muscles converge; key for support.
Pelvic organ prolapse and urinary or faecal incontinence after childbirth, ageing, straining.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ileum. Lower three fifths: narrower and thinner, with more fat in the mesentery, short vasa recta and many small arcades.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Peyer's patches. Aggregated lymphoid follicles typical of the ileum (GALT).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Jejunum. Upper two fifths: wider, thicker-walled and more vascular, with long vasa recta and few large arcades.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Plicae circulares. Circular folds, tall and numerous in the jejunum, fewer in the ileum.

title: Length and parts of the small intestine?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: Length and parts of the small intestine?
body.back: 6-7 m: duodenum 20-30 cm, jejunum ~2.5 m (2/5), ileum ~3.5 m (3/5).
Plicae circulares, villi, microvilli; enterocytes, goblet, Paneth, enteroendocrine cells.
Superior (cap), descending (major papilla), horizontal (crossed by SMA/SMV), ascending (duodenojejunal flexure, ligament of Treitz).
Coeliac (superior pancreaticoduodenal via gastroduodenal) and SMA (inferior pancreaticoduodenal).
Jejunum: wider, thicker, more vascular, long vasa recta, few arcades. Ileum: narrower, short vasa recta, many arcades, Peyer's patches.
Duodenum mostly retroperitoneal; jejunum and ileum intraperitoneal on the mesentery; ligament of Treitz.
Mesenteric infarction, obstruction, coeliac disease, Crohn's disease.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gastrosplenic ligament. From the greater curvature; carries the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pancreatic ligaments. Pancreaticosplenic and pancreaticocolic (mesocolon) folds.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Splenocolic and phrenicocolic ligaments. Parts of the greater omentum; the phrenicocolic ligament supports the lower pole.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Spleen. 10-12 cm, 150-200 g; intraperitoneal except at the hilum.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Splenophrenic ligament. To the diaphragm.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Splenorenal ligament. From the left kidney; carries the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas.
Ovoid, soft, 10-12 cm, 150-200 g; intraperitoneal except hilum; largest lymphoid mass.
Left hypochondrium against ribs 9-11, long axis along rib 10, behind the costodiaphragmatic recess; not palpable normally.
Diaphragmatic (recess, left lung) and visceral (colic flexure, pancreatic tail, stomach, kidney); hilum.
Gastrosplenic, splenophrenic, splenorenal, pancreaticosplenic, pancreaticocolic, splenocolic, phrenicocolic.
Largest coeliac branch; along upper pancreas, behind lesser sac, in splenorenal ligament; 2-3 segmental branches.
From hilum in splenorenal ligament, behind pancreas, joins SMV → portal vein.
Coeliac and SMA nodes; vagus and splanchnic nerves.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Common hepatic artery. Gives the right gastric (lesser curvature) and the gastroduodenal artery, whose right gastroepiploic branch runs along the greater curvature.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Coeliac trunk. Artery of the foregut; three branches: left gastric, common hepatic, splenic.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Greater curvature. Anastomosis of the left and right gastroepiploic arteries.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lesser curvature. Anastomosis of the left and right gastric arteries.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Left gastric artery. Runs up then along the lesser curvature; also gives oesophageal branches.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Splenic artery. Gives the left gastroepiploic artery and the short gastric arteries to the fundus.
25 cm; C6 (cricoid) to T11; hiatus at T10.
UES (air), LES (reflux); GERD (LES dysfunction), achalasia (LES fails to relax).
Non-keratinised stratified squamous mucosa, submucosal glands, muscularis (skeletal → mixed → smooth), adventitia (no serosa).
Front: trachea, left atrium. Back: vertebrae, thoracic duct, azygos. Left: aortic arch, thoracic aorta. Right: azygos, right lung.
Arteries: inferior thyroid, aortic/bronchial branches, left gastric. Veins: inferior thyroid, azygos, left gastric → portal (portosystemic).
Cardia, fundus, body, pylorus; lesser and greater curvatures.
Lesser: hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal (portal triad). Greater: gastrocolic, gastrosplenic, gastrophrenic.
Lesser curvature: left gastric + right gastric. Greater curvature: left + right gastroepiploic. Fundus: short gastrics.
Left gastric → portal; short gastrics, left gastroepiploic → splenic; right gastroepiploic → SMV.
Helicobacter pylori, NSAIDs.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Aortic bifurcation. At L4 into the right and left common iliac arteries.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Coeliac trunk. Short, thick artery at T12; left gastric, common hepatic, splenic arteries; foregut.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inferior mesenteric artery. At L3; left colic, sigmoid, superior rectal; hindgut.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lateral paired branches. Middle suprarenal, renal (just below SMA, L1-L2), and gonadal arteries (below the renals, on psoas).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Posterior branches. Inferior phrenic and lumbar arteries (at risk in aortic surgery).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Superior mesenteric artery. At L1; inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal and ileal, ileocolic, right colic, middle colic; midgut.
From the diaphragm (T12) to the bifurcation into common iliac arteries at L4.
Coeliac trunk (T12, foregut), SMA (L1, midgut), IMA (L3, hindgut).
Left gastric, common hepatic (→ gastroduodenal), splenic.

title: Branches of the SMA and IMA?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: Branches of the SMA and IMA?
body.back: SMA: inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal/ileal, ileocolic, right colic, middle colic. IMA: left colic, sigmoid, superior rectal.
Lateral: middle suprarenal, renal (L1-L2), gonadal. Posterior: inferior phrenic, lumbar.

title: Course and tributaries of the IVC?
subject: subj:anat2

body.front: Course and tributaries of the IVC?
body.back: Common iliacs at L5, right of aorta, diaphragm at T8; tributaries: iliac, lumbar, gonadal (right), renal, right suprarenal, phrenic, hepatic; none from the gut.
SMV + splenic vein (receiving IMV) + gastric veins; carries gut and spleen blood to liver sinusoids.
Oesophageal, paraumbilical, rectal, retroperitoneal; TIPS or surgical shunts for portal hypertension.
